clinicalPearls: Consider in middle-aged women with fatigue, pruritus, and an isolated cholestatic (alkaline phosphatase-predominant) liver panel
Pruritus often precedes jaundice by months to years and may be the presenting complaint
Antimitochondrial antibody (AMA) positivity at meaningful titer is highly specific and often clinches the diagnosis without biopsy
Associated with other autoimmune conditions — Sjögren syndrome, autoimmune thyroiditis, scleroderma/CREST, celiac disease
Hyperlipidemia is common but does not appear to confer the usual cardiovascular risk seen in the general population
Fat-soluble vitamin deficiency and metabolic bone disease (osteoporosis) develop as cholestasis progresses
AMA-negative patients with a compatible clinical/biochemical picture still warrant workup as 'AMA-negative PBC'
harrison.pathophysiology: PBC is an autoimmune, T-cell-mediated process that progressively destroys small and medium intrahepatic bile ducts, producing chronic cholestasis. Ongoing bile duct injury leads to periportal inflammation, fibrosis, and eventually biliary-type cirrhosis if untreated. Genetic susceptibility combined with environmental triggers is thought to break tolerance to mitochondrial autoantigens, driving the characteristic antimitochondrial antibody response.
additionalInvestigations: Alkaline phosphatase and GGT — establish and quantify cholestatic pattern
Antimitochondrial antibody (AMA) — key serologic marker, positive in most cases
Antinuclear antibody (ANA), including PBC-specific patterns (anti-gp210, anti-sp100) — useful when AMA is negative
Serum IgM — characteristically elevated in PBC
Abdominal ultrasound or cross-sectional imaging — exclude extrahepatic biliary obstruction
Liver biopsy — confirms diagnosis in AMA-negative cases and stages disease when diagnosis is uncertain
Transient elastography (FibroScan) or other noninvasive fibrosis assessment — staging and monitoring
Fat-soluble vitamin levels and bone density (DEXA) — assess complications of chronic cholestasis
redFlags: Development of jaundice, ascites, variceal bleeding, or encephalopathy signaling decompensated cirrhosis
Inadequate biochemical response to first-line therapy — warrants consideration of second-line agents and closer surveillance
New or worsening features suggesting overlap with autoimmune hepatitis
Rising alpha-fetoprotein or new liver lesion — evaluate for hepatocellular carcinoma once cirrhosis is established
Severe intractable pruritus refractory to standard measures
Symptomatic metabolic bone disease or fragility fracture
pitfalls: Attributing isolated cholestatic labs and pruritus in an older woman to cholelithiasis or aging skin without checking AMA
Assuming a negative AMA excludes PBC — a subset of patients are AMA-negative and require biopsy or specific autoantibodies
Missing an overlap syndrome by not screening for autoimmune hepatitis features when transaminases are disproportionately elevated
Overlooking screening for associated autoimmune diseases and osteoporosis once diagnosis is established
harrison.prognosis: Course is highly variable; many patients with early-stage disease and a good biochemical response to therapy have a life expectancy similar to the general population, while incomplete responders or those presenting with advanced fibrosis progress toward cirrhosis and its complications over years.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Chapter on Primary Biliary Cholangitis / Approach to the Patient with Liver Disease
management: Start ursodeoxycholic acid as first-line therapy to slow progression, assessing biochemical response after a defined interval
Add obeticholic acid or a fibrate for patients with an inadequate response to ursodeoxycholic acid
Treat pruritus stepwise with the bile acid sequestrant cholestyramine, then rifampicin, opioid antagonists such as naltrexone, or sertraline
Prevent and treat metabolic bone disease with calcium and vitamin D, bisphosphonates where indicated, and supplement deficient fat-soluble vitamins
Screen for associated autoimmune conditions including thyroid disease, coeliac disease, and Sjogren syndrome
Monitor biochemical response and disease stage, adding hepatocellular carcinoma and varices surveillance once cirrhosis develops
Refer for liver transplantation in decompensated cirrhosis or intractable pruritus
